story.title: Leon Black Sues House Committee After Skipping Epstein Deposition
story.summary: Leon Black, a billionaire and former associate of Jeffrey Epstein, did not attend a scheduled deposition before the House Oversight Committee. Instead, he filed a lawsuit against the committee, seeking to block subpoenas related to its investigation into Epstein. Black had previously been subpoenaed in June after leaving a voluntary appearance abruptly.

event_overview.title: About Epstein Investigation
event_overview.subject: Epstein Investigation
event_overview.summary: The Epstein investigation refers to a set of U.S. criminal investigations, prosecutions, custody reviews and later records-disclosure efforts concerning Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual exploitation of minors and the people or institutions connected to those matters. It includes an earlier Florida investigation and plea resolution, a 2019 federal sex-trafficking case in New York that ended after Epstein’s death, the prosecution of Ghislaine Maxwell, and subsequent government review and disclosure of related records.

facts.label: Origins and early resolution
facts.value: A federal investigation in the Southern District of Florida ran from 2006 to 2008. Epstein entered guilty pleas in Palm Beach County on June 30, 2008; DOJ later found that victims had not been treated with the expected forthrightness and sensitivity during the federal resolution process.

facts.label: 2019 federal case
facts.value: A federal grand jury in the Southern District of New York returned an indictment on July 2, 2019, charging Epstein with sex trafficking of minors and conspiracy; the indictment alleged conduct from at least 2002 through 2005 involving dozens of underage girls in New York and Palm Beach, Florida.

facts.label: Death and custody review
facts.value: Epstein died in federal custody at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City on August 10, 2019. DOJ’s inspector general issued its review of the Bureau of Prisons’ custody, care and supervision of Epstein on June 27, 2023; a later FBI review likewise concluded that his death was suicide.

facts.label: Maxwell prosecution
facts.value: Ghislaine Maxwell, described by prosecutors as Epstein’s longtime partner and co-conspirator, was convicted by a federal jury in the Southern District of New York on December 29, 2021 on five felony counts involving the sexual abuse of young girls.

facts.label: Records disclosure
facts.value: The Epstein Files Transparency Act, signed on November 19, 2025, directed DOJ to produce—with limited exceptions—records related to investigations and prosecutions of Epstein and Maxwell. DOJ’s public Epstein Library says disclosures are redacted to protect victims and may be updated if additional releasable documents are identified.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows particular 2026 developments involving alleged associates, litigation, congressional oversight and access to Epstein-related materials; it does not attempt to catalog every criminal allegation, civil case, records release or person mentioned in those materials.

explore_lenses.label: What changed beyond the missed deposition?
explore_lenses.title: The dispute is now in federal court
explore_lenses.summary: Black did not merely decline a committee appearance: on September 3 he filed suit seeking to invalidate and block enforcement of two subpoenas. The subpoenas originated in his June 26 voluntary interview, where the committee said he would not answer questions about nondisclosure agreements.

claims.text: Chair James Comer issued two subpoenas on June 26, 2026: one for Black's deposition and one for nondisclosure agreements.
Black's September 3 lawsuit asks a federal court to block the subpoenas, rather than simply seeking to negotiate their scope or timing.
The House released the transcript of Black's June 26 transcribed interview on July 17, making part of the prior exchange publicly reviewable.

Black's September 3 lawsuit asks a federal court to block the subpoenas, rather than simply seeking to negotiate their scope or timing.

explore_lenses.label: What do Black and the committee argue?
explore_lenses.title: A fight over relevance, privacy, and oversight power
explore_lenses.summary: Black's side says the demands reach private matters without a sufficient legislative connection and could expose third parties. Committee leaders say the records and testimony are pertinent to examining Epstein's influence and alleged governmental failures involving survivors.

claims.text: Black argues that the subpoenas lack a legitimate connection to the committee's legislative purpose and that producing the agreements could expose women who sought confidentiality and have no known public connection to Epstein.
Black attorney Susan Estrich characterized the inquiry as a 'fishing expedition' and an abuse of congressional power.

Comer says the committee is examining how the federal government failed Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell survivors and how Epstein sought influence; he calls Black's testimony crucial because Black was a fee-paying client and has several NDAs.
Comer previously said the committee wanted to determine whether Epstein participated in drafting or negotiating Black's NDAs or in payments connected to them.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next procedurally?
explore_lenses.title: Court litigation and possible contempt are separate tracks
explore_lenses.summary: Black's suit puts the subpoena dispute before a federal court, while the House can separately consider contempt. A contempt referral is not automatic and would not itself guarantee that the committee obtains the requested testimony or documents.

claims.text: Comer said the committee would make a record of the missed deposition and that he would consult members about next steps; Ranking Member Robert Garcia called for Black to be held in contempt.

Under the Congressional Research Service's description of the process, willful noncompliance with a congressional subpoena is addressed by 2 U.S.C. § 192, while § 194 governs referrals to the Justice Department; the House typically uses a full-chamber vote for such a referral.

A Justice Department referral does not require prosecution, and criminal contempt principally punishes and deters rather than necessarily compelling compliance; Congress can also seek civil enforcement in court.

story_report.summary: Leon Black did not appear for a scheduled deposition before the House Oversight Committee and filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block subpoenas tied to the panel’s Epstein investigation. The subpoenas seek Black’s testimony and nondisclosure agreements. Committee Chairman James Comer said the panel would formally record the missed deposition and consult members on next steps, while Ranking Member Robert Garcia called for Black to be held in contempt.

sections.heading: Black Subpoenas Follow Prior Interview
sections.body: Comer issued two subpoenas to Black on June 26, 2026: one compelling a deposition and another seeking nondisclosure agreements. The House later released the transcript of Black’s June 26 transcribed interview on July 17, making part of his earlier exchange with the committee public. The subpoena dispute therefore follows an interview that Black had already given the panel in some form.

sections.heading: Black and Comer Contest Subpoena Purpose
sections.body: Black argues that the subpoenas lack a legitimate connection to a legislative purpose and that disclosure of the agreements could expose women who sought confidentiality and have no known public connection to Epstein. His attorney, Susan Estrich, called the inquiry a “fishing expedition” and an abuse of congressional power. Comer says the investigation concerns federal failures involving Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell survivors, Epstein’s efforts to gain influence, and whether Epstein helped draft or negotiate Black’s agreements or related payments.

sections.heading: House Response Options Remain Open
sections.body: Garcia has urged that Black be held in contempt, but Comer has said only that he will consult committee members after recording the missed deposition. Under the Congressional Research Service’s description, a criminal-contempt process can involve a House vote and a referral to the Justice Department, though a referral does not require prosecution and principally serves punitive and deterrent purposes. Congress may also pursue civil enforcement in court.

unresolved.text: The consulted reporting did not establish whether a court had scheduled a hearing or issued an interim order in Black’s lawsuit by September 3.

As of September 3, the consulted sources identified no House contempt vote, Justice Department referral, or court ruling; a court will determine whether the subpoenas serve a valid legislative purpose and what protections may apply to the requested records.

related_stories.title: Giorgia Meloni's Government Becomes Italy's Longest-Serving Since WWII
related_stories.summary: Giorgia Meloni's administration has surpassed 1,413 consecutive days in office, making it the longest-lasting government in Italy's postwar history. This milestone surpasses the previous record held by Silvio Berlusconi's second administration. Meloni, Italy's first female Prime Minister, has governed since 2022, navigating both domestic and international challenges.

related_stories.title: Putin Dismisses Need for New Mobilization Amid Peace Talks
related_stories.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin stated there is currently no need for additional mobilization in the Ukraine war, labeling such reports as Ukrainian disinformation. He made these comments during an economic forum in eastern Russia. Additionally, Putin expressed optimism about the possibility of reaching a peace agreement, while Kyiv noted it anticipates a 'new dynamic' in peace efforts.

related_stories.title: Maltese Tycoon Acquitted in Journalist Murder Case, Activist Expresses Devastation
related_stories.summary: A Maltese tycoon has been acquitted of orchestrating the murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, who was killed by a car bomb in 2017. Tom Gibson, Deputy Director for the Committee to Protect Journalists, expressed his devastation over the not guilty verdict, highlighting the ongoing struggle for justice in cases involving attacks on journalists.
